title: Bolton care home nurse dragged patient to floor, cutting his head

input.lead: David Guyers was struck off by the regulator after lying to cover up his behaviour
input.summary: David Guyers was struck off by the regulator after lying to cover up his behaviour
input.evidence_text: Bolton care home nurse dragged patient to floor, cutting his head - BBC News Image source, Google Image caption, David Guyers gave a dishonest account of what happened By Jonny Humphries North West Published 1 hour ago A nurse pulled a vulnerable resident at a care home for people with mental health conditions to the ground causing him to cut his head, a misconduct panel heard. David Guyers, who worked at Swallowfield Garden Care Home in Bolton, also lied in an incident report in which he described the man as sustaining a "witnessed fall". An independent panel heard Guyers claimed the man, referred to as Resident A, had been "trashing the kitchen" and that he tried to take hold of his hands to remove him. However, Guyers was struck off after the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) watchdog reviewed CCTV footage confirming Resident A's behaviour "appeared to give no cause for concern". The panel heard that Resident A was allowed access to the kitchen and had personal food items in a shared fridge. The NMC found that on 22 February 2023, during a night shift, Guyers approached the resident in the kitchen and the two appeared to speak for less than a minute. It said: "Mr Guyers grabbed Resident A by the arm and pulled or dragged him across the kitchen, causing Resident A to fall to the floor, partly into the corridor. 'Untoward behaviour' "It was also alleged that Resident A sustained a head injury, with visible bleeding from a cut to the forehead." It said Resident A was known to "become anxious and unsettled" by "change or unfamiliar situations". He could present as "hostile or verbally aggressive", but it was "very rare" for Resident A to become physically aggressive. "He was shouting all sorts and one of them started running off while the other stayed oddly quite close to me." title: Slugs to blame for mystery of faulty Stretford traffic lights

input.lead: Highways bosses were initially baffled about the cause of the issue until the slimy culprit was revealed
input.summary: Highways bosses were initially baffled about the cause of the issue until the slimy culprit was revealed
input.evidence_text: Slugs to blame for mystery of faulty Stretford traffic lights - BBC News Image source, BBC/PA Image caption, The slugs had been crawling into traffic light wiring, causing short circuits By Ed Barnes Local Democracy Reporting Service Published 1 October 2026 The mystery of why malfunctioning traffic lights have been causing chaos for motorists for weeks has been revealed - and it turns out slugs are to blame. Despite being fixed or replaced, the lights at the Robin Hood crossroads in Stretford, Trafford, have repeatedly failed, with three dangerous incidents reported in the space of a year. Engineers were initially baffled, but Transport for Greater Manchester has now found the issues were caused by slugs "entering the signal controller, causing short circuits", the Local Democracy Reporting Service said. "This was the first time the highways team had ever experienced this," said Councillor Steve Adshead. It is thought the slugs were crawling inside the traffic lights for warmth, before being killed by the electrical systems which power the lights. "For them to go several times less than a couple of years old seemed very odd," Adshead said. "We had a couple of residents raise it with us saying 'why do these lights keep going?' "I had to push Transport for Greater Manchester on it quite a bit." title: Manchester Piccadilly street food traders 'sad to lose home'

input.lead: Manchester Piccadilly Market is to close as the redevelopment of Piccadilly Gardens begins
input.summary: Manchester Piccadilly Market is to close as the redevelopment of Piccadilly Gardens begins
input.evidence_text: Manchester Piccadilly street food traders 'sad to lose home' - BBC News Image caption, Leya and Olivia Linsdell said they hope the change will bring new opportunities By Elle McDade North West Published 1 October 2026 Street food traders have said they are "sad to lose their home" as Manchester Piccadilly Market prepares to close for the redevelopment of Piccadilly Gardens. The market will shut on 22 October as part of Manchester City Council's multi-million-pound revamp. Traders said they were disappointed to leave a site where they had built a loyal customer base and strong community. The council said all traders would be offered alternative locations. Image caption, Rita's Reign has 25 employees Leya Linsdell, 32, deputy operations manager at family-run Afro-Caribbean food stall Rita's Reign, said she was "incredibly disappointed" after seven years at the site. "We're a family-run business. It's just my mum, dad, sister and me," she said. She said uncertainty over the relocation was worrying, with more than 25 employees relying on the business for their income. 'There will be losses' "It's hard not being able to tell our staff what's going to happen with their jobs, and it's hard for us to make long-term decisions," Linsdell said. Her sister Olivia Linsdell, 30, said: "The change will impact us. There will be losses." While she agreed the area could benefit from the scheme, she said she was concerned the revamp could "take away Manchester's independent businesses". Image caption, A worker at BangGaBangGa, a Korean food vendor fears regular customers will go elsewhere The market is home to traders including Chen's Happy House, BangGaBangGa and Loaded Gyros. input.summary: Hopwood DePree took the council to court in his bid to take over the Grade II-listed mansion for £1

title: 'The mystery we all want solved': what's with all the corn on Market Street?

input.lead: Every morning at 11 almost exactly on the dot, a group of men gather on the ground floor of the Northern Quarter Car Park: that tall, graffiti-coated building on the corner of Church and Tib Street One by one they unlock the padlocks dangling from the back of their flat-tyred van
input.summary: Every morning at 11 almost exactly on the dot, a group of men gather on the ground floor of the Northern Quarter Car Park: that tall, graffiti-coated building on the corner of Church and Tib Street One by one they unlock the padlocks dangling from the back of their flat-tyred van
input.evidence_text: Every morning at 11 almost exactly on the dot, a group of men gather on the ground floor of the Northern Quarter Car Park: that tall, graffiti-coated building on the corner of Church and Tib Street One by one they unlock the padlocks dangling from the back of their flat-tyred vans, and the doors swing open. Out from within comes cart after cart full of corn This is the not-entirely-secret HQ of the Market Street corn vendors: a four-storey council-owned car park, sitting across two of Manchester’s busiest streets. When I get there, the men are working in silence, hands sheathed in black gloves, bags of sweetcorn torn open, cardboard Just as I’m about to approach a vendor, I’m forwarded an email from a reader. It has the subject line The Mystery We All Want Solved "The reason I’m writing is because the people of Manchester are desperate to know what the hell is going on with all of the corn sellers on Market St "Why are there now so many of them? How on earth do they make a profit? Are they independent vendors or all part of the same company? Is their presence legal? What does their proliferation say about the state of the city centre?”

Different regions have different strengths, assets and specialisms, and there was a strong view that greater collaboration between places could create bi Procurement and buying local also featured strongly. The discussion highlighted the role public sector buying power can play in supporting regional businesses, helping successful pilots move into commercial contracts and strengthening UK capability in areas such as AI and cyber There was also a broader conversation about sovereignty and the UK’s role internationally. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: A unique classical concert which aims to improve the experience of people with hearing loss who want to enjoy music is coming to Manchester this October Academics from the Cadenza Project, working with the Manchester Camerata orchestra, are inviting people with and without hearing loss to a special research show at the Stoller Hall on Thu 29 Oct. The concert will feature Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6, the Pastoral Symphony The Cadenza project, led by the University of Salford, is researching how to improve music for people with hearing loss. The free concert is a unique opportunity to shape future research on hearing aids while enjoying live music Trevor Cox, Professor of acoustic engineering at the University of Salford, explains: “We don’t think anything like this has been attempted before. When people suffer hearing loss, the main treatment is a hearing aid. But the devices are designed for speech. Music is an afterthou “But music is such an important part of our lives, it brings us together for shared experiences that people with hearing issues can feel locked out of. Live classical music is particularly hard for hearing aids to deal with, as it ranges from extremely quiet to very louder, over “This is a unique opportunity for people, both with hearing problems and those who hear normally, to help shape future research on hearing aids while enjoying the fabulous Camerata.”

input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
